title: Analysis
text: ANALYSIS THE OLD AND THE NEW At the heart of Ishiguro’s text is the conflict between tradition and modernity, old and new. Stevens is an effective character through whom we can consider this conflict because he is a butler in a grand English house – a profession rooted in tradition which in today’s world strikes us as somewhat outdated. Writing in 1956, Stevens claims that the professionalism of the past is “almost impossible to find nowadays” (p. 9). The disappearance of professionalism that Stevens notes is representative of a wider general progression from a traditional society to a modern one. One of the ways that Ishiguro illustrates this transition is with reference to honour and loyalty. Just as Stevens believes that it is honourable to remain loyal to his employer Lord Darlington, Lord Darlington deems it morally sound to remain trustworthy to his German political associates. Lord Darlington’s confidence in the German nation facilitates the Nazis’ rise to power, and this is a clear error of judgement. During one of the international conferences hosted at Darlington Hall, an American gentleman named Mr Lewis accuses Darlington and his colleagues of being amateurs in the sphere of international affairs. He bitingly announces, “the days when you could act out of your noble instincts are over” (p. 102). Mr Lewis asserts that in the world in which they now find themselves, doing what is right does not necessarily mean doing what is noble and morally virtuous. In this way, Ishiguro presents the malfunctioning of a generation that places the values of honour and loyalty over those of retaliation, cunning negotiation and pragmatism. It is significant that Mr Lewis, an adversary of Lord Darlington, is from the USA. Another way in which Ishiguro presents the change in world society is through the division between the USA and the UK. Both of the American characters in the novel, Mr Lewis and Mr Farraday, present an opposition or contrast to the old-fashioned Lord Darlington, and thus we can associate the themes and values that these characters are associated with to the emerging modern world: realism, hard-headedness, informality, attachment to money, and so on. MEMORIES The Remains of the Day is structured in the form of a diary. The reader does not see the action unfold as it happens, but rather sees the events of the story through the window of Stevens’ memories. It is very important to acknowledge that all the episodes of the novel have passed through the filter of one character and that this shapes the way that the text presents itself. Stevens is an exceptionally cool, composed and rational character, and thus it is no surprise that the narrative is balanced, not paced too quickly, and logical in terms of the sequence of events that is narrated; the novel intersperses memories with descriptions of the present moment that complement one another in a perfectly balanced way. Stevens is also an emotionally complex character, and this is perhaps the most interesting facet of his character revealed by his narration. Given that Stevens places professionalism over the acknowledgement of his own emotions, at moments when he is emotionally susceptible, he refuses to express his grief and we only learn of it through the dialogue of other characters. For example, when his father falls ill, Stevens continues working and does not comment on it at all. The only way we learn that Stevens is sad is because Lord Darlington remarks “you look as though you’re crying” (p. 105). The refusal to mention his own feelings is a very effective way of showing how this character supresses his emotions, allowing their only manifestation to be involuntary (tears). LOVE AND PROFESSIONALISM Love and professionalism are two pivotal themes in this text because they offer a conflict. In Stevens’ world, there is not a shadow of a doubt that romantic pursuit runs contrary to being a professional. But this tightly-held belief does not prevent him from internally yearning for Miss Kenton. ‘Internally’ is crucial here, because not once does Stevens permit himself the space to openly reflect upon his feelings for Miss Kenton. As he says, if a butler is to be ‘great’, then the only time that he lays his professionalism to one side is when he is completely alone; Stevens is aware of the presence of his reader and so never strays from fully inhabiting his role. Because of this, we must read into the implications of Stevens’ words and actions. He coats his flirtation with Miss Kenton in the guise of professionalism, for example their “cocoa evenings”, in which they would begin discussing work matters before drifting into more “harmless” trivial ones, “which did much, one should say, to relieve the many tensions produced by a hard day” (p. 157). More than simply “relieving the tensions of a hard day”, Stevens is communicating that he enjoys passing a relaxed time in her presence; it is something that makes him happy. The reader must decipher such comments because Stevens only speaks in terms of how something affects his work, and never in terms of how it makes him happy or unhappy. Like all humans, Stevens is an emotional being, but because of the extremely high professional standards he sets himself he has no outlet for emotional expression. As a result, we can only detect it surfacing in specific infrequent moments, such as when Stevens is caught reading a sentimental love story. He is clearly embarrassed when Miss Kenton intrudes into his study and demands to know what he is reading, because he is reluctant to show her the book’s title. When he eventually reveals that he is a reading a sentimental romance he rationalises it with reference to his work, saying that it improves his spoken command of the English language, a quality that all great butlers must possess. Just as Stevens justifies his cocoa evenings with Miss Kenton by affirming that they are essential to the proper running of the household, and his trip to Cornwall by claiming that it is to remedy the understaffing problem at Darlington Hall, he justifies reading the romance novel in relation to his profession. In other words, Stevens supresses his emotions by subordinating them to the professional needs of his work.
